The most important thing to understand is that every child inherits exactly 50 percent of their DNA from each parent — not roughly, not on average, but precisely. What varies enormously is *which* 50 percent of each parent's genome that child receives, and it is this randomness in the shuffling process that explains why siblings typically share only about half of their DNA with each other, why half-siblings share only a quarter, and why identical twins, despite their name, can still end up with subtle genetic differences that matter for disease and traits.

The shuffling happens in two distinct stages during meiosis, and both are essential to understanding sibling DNA sharing. The first stage is **independent assortment**, which occurs during Metaphase I of meiosis. At this moment, each of the 23 pairs of homologous chromosomes lines up along the cell's equator, and each pair decides independently whether the maternal or the paternal chromosome will travel into each daughter cell. There is a fifty-fifty chance for each pair, and because all 23 pairs make this decision independently, the total number of possible chromosome combinations in a single gamete is 2 raised to the 23rd power — roughly 8.4 million unique possibilities from one person. This number alone explains why two siblings can receive radically different genetic packages from the same parents, even before considering the second stage of shuffling.

The second stage is **crossing over**, which occurs during Prophase I, specifically at a substage called the pachytene phase. Here, homologous chromosomes pair up so tightly that they form a structure called a tetrad, and at various points along their length, they break and exchange equal segments of DNA with each other. The result is a recombinant chromosome — one that carries maternal alleles on what started as a paternal chromosome, or vice versa. Each human gamete experiences an average of about 26 crossovers per meiosis, and critically, the positions of those crossovers differ from one meiotic event to the next. One sperm cell might carry a recombination event at a particular position on chromosome 3, while the very next sperm cell from the same man might have no crossover there at all. This means that each gamete produced by the same individual is genetically unique, and this is why siblings inherit not just different chromosomes but different *versions* of the same chromosome.

When a child is conceived, they receive 23 chromosomes from their mother and 23 from their father, giving them a complete diploid genome. A sibling goes through the exact same process with the same parents, receiving 23 chromosomes from each as well. The naive expectation might be that siblings therefore share all of their DNA, since they draw from the same two pools. But the shuffling mechanisms described above make this impossible. Each child receives a randomly sampled 50 percent of their mother's genetic variation and a randomly sampled 50 percent of their father's, and those two samples do not coincide. For any given allele that a parent carries, there is a 50 percent chance that Child A inherits it and a 50 percent chance that Child B inherits it. The probability that both children inherit the same allele at that locus is therefore 0.5 times 0.5, which equals 0.25, or 25 percent. But because the genome contains many loci, and because recombination further mixes them within chromosomes, the aggregate effect across the whole genome averages out to approximately 50 percent shared DNA between full siblings.

That word "approximately" is doing real work here. The actual amount of shared DNA between full siblings ranges from roughly 35 to 65 percent, according to multiple sources in the genealogical and genetics literature. This range exists because recombination shuffles the deck differently for each child, and the specific outcome of that shuffle is subject to chance. One sibling might happen to inherit a disproportionately large share of their paternal grandmother's DNA on chromosome 7, while their brother inherits a different combination. Over the full genome, these random differences accumulate, producing the observed variation around the 50 percent mean.

The case of half-siblings makes the logic even clearer. Two half-siblings share only one parent. From that shared parent, they each still receive 50 percent of their genome, but the overlap in what they each receive averages only 25 percent, because for any given allele from the shared parent, there is only a one-in-four chance that both children inherited the same version. The other half of each child's genome comes from an unrelated parent, contributing no expected shared DNA. This is why half-siblings share roughly 25 percent of their DNA — essentially half of what full siblings share — and why this figure can overlap with the range seen for other relationships like grandparents, aunts, and uncles, which also share approximately 25 percent by a different genealogical route.

One of the most important nuances emerging from recent research is that recombination is not evenly distributed across the genome. Crossovers cluster in short regions called recombination hotspots, where they occur far more frequently than in surrounding sequence, and they are conspicuously rare at centromeres and other structural regions. The primary determinant of hotspot location in humans and mice is a gene called **PRDM9**, which encodes a protein that binds to specific 13-base-pair DNA motifs and marks those sites for the recombination machinery. Different alleles of PRDM9 shift where hotspots sit, explaining roughly 40 percent of the variation in hotspot localization across populations. This means that two siblings might inherit the same chromosomal segment from a parent, but if recombination occurs at different positions within that segment in their father's versus their mother's meiosis, the boundaries of what they share can differ substantially.

The implications for predictability are significant. Regions of the genome that experience many crossovers — such as chromosome ends near telomeres — get broken into small pieces with each generation. Alleles in these regions travel with different flanking markers in each sibling, making their inheritance less predictable. In contrast, regions with few crossovers, like centromeric cores, tend to travel as large, intact haplotype blocks across many generations. An allele sitting in a centromeric region is far more likely to be transmitted together with its surrounding markers, producing more predictable inheritance patterns. Furthermore, recombination rates differ between the sexes. Female meiosis typically produces more total crossovers than male meiosis, and the hotspots themselves are located in different genomic contexts depending on whether the recombining cell is in a male or a female body. This means that the same chromosome can be more shuffled when inherited from the mother and more conserved when inherited from the father.

The concept of identical twins provides a natural experiment that sharpens understanding of all the mechanisms described above. Identical twins originate from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos, meaning they start with an identical nuclear genome. For many years, researchers treated them as genetically uniform controls for studying environmental effects on traits and disease. But the evidence now shows that identical twins are not perfectly identical at the DNA level, and the differences reveal something important about the forces shaping sibling genetic similarity more broadly.

Studies that have sequenced the genomes of large numbers of identical twin pairs have found that post-zygotic mutations — genetic changes that occur after the twins have split from one another — accumulate at measurable rates. In one study of 381 Icelandic twin pairs, the median number of mutations differing between twins within a pair was 14, though some pairs showed over 100 differences while others showed essentially none. These are not epigenetic modifications but actual changes in DNA sequence, arising from errors in DNA replication during the many cell divisions that follow the twinning event. The rate of such mutations is not fixed. Research in mice has identified specific genetic variants, such as alleles near a gene called *Mutyh*, that can increase the per-generation point mutation rate by as much as 50 percent. Environmental exposures — tobacco smoke, UV radiation, ionizing radiation — are known to leave characteristic mutational signatures in the genome and to increase somatic mutation burdens in exposed tissues. And paternal age is a dominant factor in germline mutation rate, with each additional year of paternal age adding approximately one to two new mutations to the genome that gets passed to children.

Despite all this, post-zygotic mutations between identical twins matter far less for the question of sibling DNA sharing than recombination does. The reason is one of scale. Each generation of meiosis involves roughly 26 crossover events per gamete, compared to approximately 74 new point mutations per genome per generation in the germline. Recombination events are therefore hundreds of times more frequent than new mutations, and each crossover has a far larger effect on breaking up or preserving shared haplotype blocks between relatives. Mutations do change the exact sequence within those blocks, but they do not alter the fundamental pattern of which chromosomal segments siblings share. For identity-by-descent analysis — the method that population geneticists use to measure how much DNA two individuals inherited from a recent common ancestor — recombination is the dominant force, and mutation contributes only a small amount of noise at the level of individual nucleotides.

Another layer of complexity comes from the fact that recombination does not just determine similarity between siblings; it determines the entire architecture of genetic inheritance across generations. The length of a shared chromosomal segment between two relatives is inversely proportional to the number of meioses separating them from their most recent common ancestor. A segment shared between siblings, who are separated from each parent by two meioses, has an expected average length of about one-quarter of a chromosome (or roughly 25 centiMorgans per segment). First cousins, separated by six meioses from their shared grandparents, share shorter segments on average. As you go further back in a family tree, recombination has had more opportunities to break the ancestral chromosomes into smaller and smaller pieces, and the IBD segments become correspondingly shorter and more numerous.

This is why genealogical DNA matching works — the number and length of IBD segments between two people can reveal their relationship with remarkable precision, because the expected pattern of recombination has been well characterized. But it also explains why the precision of these methods depends on the recombination map being accurate. Because recombination hotspots vary between individuals, between sexes, and between populations, the standard population-average genetic maps used in most analyses are approximations. Researchers are now developing personalized genetic maps that capture an individual's own recombination landscape, which will improve the accuracy of relationship inference and could eventually help identify individuals at elevated risk for aneuploidies or other meiotic errors.

What emerges from all of this is a picture of meiosis as a sophisticated shuffling engine with several interacting components operating at different scales. Independent assortment determines the broad chromosomal composition of each gamete, producing the 2^23 basic possibilities. Crossing over then takes each of those possibilities and introduces additional diversity by swapping material between homologous chromosomes at specific positions, creating recombinant chromosomes that carry new combinations of alleles. The distribution of those crossover events is not random — it is shaped by genetic factors like PRDM9, modulated by the sex of the individual, and varies from person to person. Over the course of a human lifetime and across generations, this process creates a continuous stream of novel genetic combinations, which is why no two siblings — even identical twins — are genetically identical.

The 50 percent figure for full siblings and the 25 percent figure for half-siblings are not arbitrary numbers but the mathematical consequence of this shuffling process, derived from the probability that both siblings inherit the same parental allele at each locus. The range around those averages reflects the inherent randomness of recombination, the specific positions of crossover events in each meiosis, and the cumulative effect of post-zygotic mutations that diverge after twins split or after siblings develop in utero. And the fact that recombination is concentrated in hotspots and varies by sex adds a layer of structural complexity that makes some parts of the genome more predictable in their transmission than others — centromeres and telomeres behave differently, males and females shuffle their chromosomes differently, and individuals with different PRDM9 variants place their recombination machinery at different addresses.

In the end, the answer to how much DNA siblings inherit in common is not a single number but a probabilistic story written by the intersection of independent assortment, crossing over, PRDM9-driven hotspot localization, post-zygotic mutation, and the sex-specific architecture of meiosis itself. The shuffling is what makes siblings both recognizably family and undeniably individuals.
